title: The transformations of mind (3.9–3.15)
hook: even stillness is a kind of change, and the same mark can mean one, ten or a hundred depending on where it stands

segments.voice: Yesterday: prajna and samyama: concentration, meditation and absorption braided on one thing, and wisdom's light begins to shine.

Write the number one on a piece of paper. A single upright stroke. Now put a zero after it. Same stroke, same ink, and it means ten. Add another zero: a hundred. The stroke didn't grow. Nothing about it changed, and yet what it means changed completely, just by where it stands. The classical commentary on the Yoga Sutras uses this very example, to explain how things change, including the mind.
screen: `ONE STROKE OF A PEN.` → `ONE, TEN, A HUNDRED.` → `THE STROKE NEVER CHANGED.`

segments.voice: The word is parinama: transformation, change of form. Patanjali starts with the mind. Sutra 3.9: even stillness is a change. A scattering impression fades, a stilling impression rises, and the mind shifts toward quiet. Sutra 3.10: practiced again and again, that shift becomes a calm, steady flow. Then 3.11: scatteredness wanes, one-pointedness rises. And 3.12: the thought that fades and the thought that rises become alike, the same object, moment after moment. That's one-pointedness, described as a kind of change. Then he widens the lens. Sutra 3.13: the same three changes run through everything, the elements and the senses too: change of property, change of time, change of condition. Besides the stroke of the pen, the commentary gives another picture: the same woman is called mother, daughter and sister, depending on who's speaking. Sutra 3.14 names what stays underneath: the substance that carries the properties, past, present and still to come. And 3.15: a different order produces a different change. The commentary's example is clay. A lump becomes a pot. The pot breaks into shards. The shards become dust. The clay is there the whole way through. Why put this in a book on meditation? Because to do samyama on anything, you need to see clearly what changes and what carries the change. And in the Yoga Sutras' wider picture, the seer itself doesn't change at all. Only the seen does.
screen: `PARINAMA: TRANSFORMATION.` · `EVEN STILLNESS IS A CHANGE.` · `MOTHER, DAUGHTER, SISTER.` · `CLAY: LUMP, POT, SHARDS, DUST.` · then, large: `WHAT CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Rest on the breath and watch a thought arise, stay a moment and fade, then the next, without following its story. Notice the breath rising and fading too. Then notice what doesn't seem to rise and fade, the watching itself, and stay with that for a few breaths.
Parinama, change of form. Even stillness and one-pointedness are changes, carried by something that stays.
Your line: what changes. Lump, pot, shards, dust, and the clay all the way through. See you tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 467 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: KNOWLEDGE OF PAST AND FUTURE.`

howItsDone: Students of the Yoga Sutras study the transformations of 3.9–3.15 with the classical commentary, and in meditation practitioners watch thoughts arise and fade as a way of seeing change clearly.

fork.setup: you're holding a lump of clay. it becomes a pot, then breaks into shards. what has changed?
options: the form and stage; the clay is still there.
fork.reveal: the commentary's example: lump, pot, shards, dust. properties come and go; the substance that carries them stays (3.14–3.15).

original.note: Sanskrit pariṇāma: transformation, change of form; three kinds in 3.9–3.12 and three more in 3.13.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation stops the mind from changing.
what it means: stillness and focus are themselves changes, and everything changes in property, time and condition while the substance underneath remains.
what a scholar hears: nirodha-, samadhi- and ekagrata-parinama (3.9–3.12); dharma-, lakshana- and avastha-parinama (3.13); the Bhashya's numeral by place value and the clay.
recall: resting upon: following after a memory
guess: a fixed fate that can never be altered
a ritual that turns clay into a sacred pot

chat.says: Why does a meditation book spend time on how clay turns into pots?
options: To do samyama on anything, you need to see what changes and what carries the change.
Because Patanjali wanted yogis to work with clay as part of their training.
Because pottery was a sacred craft, and the sutras honor it with an example.
chat.meaning: Sutras 3.9 to 3.15 describe change: the clay stays through lump, pot and shards. Samyama needs a clear view of what changes and what carries it.

samyama.meaning: concentration, meditation and absorption held on one object
